intro: The House Position Test is kind 1a of the Memory Test, Test 1 of the RRB ALP CBAT. In the hall it has 24 questions in 8 minutes, as two parts of 12. Each part gives 2 minutes to study a map and 2 minutes to answer. You memorise where each house stands on a map of roads and landmarks, then name the letter at each house's place. It measures memory for position: each house must be tied to the spot where it stood.

On the study screen a map appears: roads, a few landmarks and the houses in their places. When its clock ends, the test screen opens. The same map returns with letters where the houses stood, and the houses sit numbered below it. You click the letter at each house's old place and press Save & Next. This page gives the screen flow, a method for both stages, the RDSO guideline's example and a 7-day plan.

method.h: Fix the frame before the houses
method.p: Read the roads and the landmarks first: how each road runs, where the well or the tree stands. The lettered map keeps the roads and every landmark.

method.h: Give every house an address
method.p: Walk the map in one order, for example the upper road left to right, then the lower road. Name each house by its neighbours: the house beside the well, the second one past the school. An address holds better than a picture.

method.h: Test yourself before the clock ends
method.p: In the last part of the 2 minutes, look away from the map and recall silently where each house stands. Any house you cannot place gets one more look. At zero the map is gone.

method.h: Go house, address, letter
method.p: Read the numbered house and recall its address. Find that spot on the lettered map, read the letter, click it and press Save & Next. If a house will not come back, click the likeliest letter and move on.

tips.h: Give houses in open ground a fuller address
tips.p: A house in open ground between two landmarks is harder to hold. Give it a fuller address, such as halfway between the well and the bend, and a second look before the clock ends.

tips.h: Count the houses on each road
tips.p: Hold a count for each road, for example three on the upper and two on the lower. A count is quick to hold and catches a house placed on the wrong road. On the test map, count along each road the same way before you click.

tips.h: Start with the odd house
tips.p: If one house stands apart, larger, alone, at a corner or at the end of a road, fix that one first. Place the rest around it.

tips.h: Notice how the houses differ
tips.p: The houses below the test map are shown by their look, numbered. Note what sets each apart before the study clock ends, so the right house goes to the right place. Two swapped houses cost two questions.

tips.h: Go to the spot, not to the letters
tips.p: On the test screen do not read the five letters first. Recall the house's address, find that spot on the map, and take the letter standing there. Reading A to E first invites a guess.

mistakes: Staring at the whole map at once instead of reading it road by road.
Memorising the houses as pictures without tying each one to a landmark.
Marking a neighbour's letter because two houses on the same road were learnt as one spot.
Carrying the Part 1 map into Part 2 and placing a new house where an old one stood.
Spending the Part 2 study time regretting Part 1 instead of reading the new map.

method.h: Say every pair as a short line
method.p: A bare number slips away before the test screen opens. Give each picture a line that holds its number: the bell rang 75 times, the key opens room 93.

method.h: Go through the pairs in rounds
method.p: Walk the 21 once in order, saying each line. Walk them again and stop only at the pairs that slipped. Three minutes allows several rounds.

method.h: Cover the numbers and check
method.p: With the study time nearly over, look at each picture and say its line without reading the number. A pair that fails gets your last seconds; the rest you leave alone.

method.h: Test page: picture, line, number
method.p: Look at the picture, say its line, and the number comes with it. Find it among A to D, click its radio and press Save & Next. If the line will not come, strike the numbers you never saw and choose among the rest.

tips.h: Keep the two digits in order
tips.p: Seventy-five is one word; seven and five are two, and two can swap. The example offers both 39 and 93 as options in one question. Hear every number as one word and the swapped option will not tempt you.

tips.h: Tie the number to the picture, not to the place
tips.p: The test page shuffles the pictures. A number remembered as the third in the row is lost once the row changes. Start every line from the picture itself.

tips.h: Give look-alike pictures a line that separates them
tips.p: Where two pictures look alike, their numbers get crossed. Put the difference into the line, so that each picture claims its own number. Give these pairs your later rounds.

tips.h: Strike the far numbers first
tips.p: Two of the four options usually sit far from any number you studied. Strike them at once, then choose between the two that are close. The close pair is where a swapped digit hides, so say the line before you look.

tips.h: Keep under 9 seconds a picture
tips.p: 21 answers in 3 minutes leaves no time for a second visit. If a picture will not give up its number, mark the likeliest and move on. The clock closes Part 1 either way.

mistakes: Looking at the pairs without saying them, then recognising every picture and knowing no number.
Learning the numbers by their place on the study screen, which the test screen shuffles.
Reading the four options before recalling the line, so that a familiar-looking number chooses itself.
Carrying a Part 1 number into Part 2 and giving it to a new picture.
Returning to a picture whose number would not come, so the clock closes the part with the last pictures blank.

method.h: Read the track before the names
method.p: Trace the lines first: the main line, where each branch leaves it, and which line is which gauge. The track stays unchanged on the test map. A station fixed to its line and junction can be found after its name has gone.

method.h: Give each station a place on the line
method.p: Travel the map like a train, in one fixed order: the main line, then each branch from its junction. Name each station by line and position: SOK, top of the branch; DET, main line, to the right. A phrase said once comes back with the name; a silent look at the map does not.

method.h: Close the map in your head
method.p: In the last moments, run the track from memory: junction, first station, second. Give your final look to the name you cannot recall; after zero there is no map to check.

method.h: From the question list to the letter
method.p: Take the name from the question and say its phrase. Ride the track with the mouse pointer to that dot; the letter sitting there is the answer. Click that option and press Save & Next.

tips.h: Make the junction your anchor
tips.p: The point where a branch leaves the main line is found at once. Count stations from it: first past the junction, second up the branch.

tips.h: Use the gauge as a landmark
tips.p: Broad gauge and metre gauge are drawn with different sleepers. A station on the thin line cannot sit on the thick one, so the gauge halves your search.

tips.h: Count the dots, named or not
tips.p: The test map keeps every dot and letters the unnamed ones too. If the names sat on the first, third and fifth dots, the letters you need sit on those dots.

tips.h: Fix the ends of each line first
tips.p: A terminus is the easiest dot to place, because the line stops there. Pin the last station on each branch first, then fit the middle names between the junction and the end.

tips.h: Start Part 2 with an empty map
tips.p: During the summary, drop the first map; nothing from it is asked again. Find the second map's junctions first.

tips.h: Run down the name list first
tips.p: On the test screen the names stand in a list beside the map. Read the list once and say each station's phrase before the first question. A name you cannot place is then known before its 10 seconds begin, and gets its likeliest letter at once.

Looking for a station's shape on the test map, where every station is the same dot.
Picking a letter from memory without tracing the track to the dot, and landing one dot off.
Dwelling on an unsure station while the last names of the part go unanswered.

method.h: Join the two shapes into one picture
method.p: Do not hold a circle and a triangle as two things. Put the triangle inside the circle, the star on the square, the arrow through the cross. One joined picture is one memory, and it comes back whole.

method.h: Give the joined picture a two-word name
method.p: Say circle-triangle, square-star, cross-arrow under your breath. Say each name both ways, triangle-circle as well, so that either shape calls up the other. The name gives the pair a second home, in sound.

method.h: Walk the pairs in rounds, then self-test
method.p: Go through all 20 once, joining and naming. Go again, stopping only where the picture would not form. Before the clock ends, look only at the first shape of each pair, say its partner, then check.

method.h: On the test screen: shape, picture, partner
method.p: Look at the shape at the left and let the joined picture form; the partner is inside it. Click its radio and press Save & Next. If nothing forms, strike the options that belong with another shape and choose among the rest.

tips.h: Fix the awkward pairs first
tips.p: A circle with a triangle joins at once; a crescent with a diamond resists. Join the awkward pairs in your first round, while attention is fresh, and check them again in your last.

tips.h: Familiar is not the same as paired
tips.p: In the RDSO guideline's example every option for the circle is a partner from the study screen. Trust the joined picture, never the feeling of having seen a shape before.

tips.h: Join to the outline, not to the name
tips.p: A square and a diamond share a name family and get crossed. Join the partner to the outline you see, the tilt of the diamond, the points of the star, so that the picture, not the word, carries the pair.

tips.h: Count the rows on your first pass
tips.p: The 20 pairs fill the study screen in rows. Count them once so you know how many pictures you must hold, and on the last pass check that every row has a joined picture. A row never reached is a blind guess on the test screen.

tips.h: Give each item 9 seconds and keep moving
tips.p: Twenty answers in 3 minutes is 9 seconds each. At item 10, Time Left should read about a minute and a half. If it reads less, stop waiting for pictures and click the first shape that fits.

mistakes: Memorising the shapes one by one, so that every shape looks familiar and no partner is known.
Picking the option you remember seeing, instead of the one that stood beside the given shape on the study screen.
Learning a pair by its place on the study screen, which is no use once the shape stands alone.
Answering a Part 2 shape with the partner its look-alike had in Part 1.
Waiting for a picture to form on one item while the clock takes the last rows of the part.

method.h: Turn each set into a code word
method.p: Read the shapes in their order and take one letter from each: square, circle, triangle becomes SCT. Say it once under your breath. A code word keeps the order; a mental picture often loses it.

method.h: Study in three passes
method.p: First pass: code every set. Second pass: say each code with its shapes. Third pass: only the sets that did not stick. Watch Time Left; the screen closes at zero, ready or not.

method.h: Strike before you pick
method.p: Strike any of the five sets with a shape you never saw. Among the rest, read the shapes in order and spell their code. The option whose code matches a studied code, letter for letter, is the answer.

method.h: Click, Save & Next, do not return
method.p: Click the radio button, press Save & Next and let the question go. Twelve answers in 2 minutes come from steady movement, not certainty.

tips.h: Give each shape its own letter
tips.p: In the RDSO guideline's example, square and star both begin with S, and circle and cross with C. So SCT and SCD differ by one letter only. Give each shape its own letter, for example R for star and X for cross, and keep it on every paper.

tips.h: The first shape removes most options
tips.p: Wrong sets often reuse the studied shapes in another order. After the strike, compare each option's first shape with the code's first letter; most fall away.

tips.h: Let go of Part 1 before Part 2
tips.p: Part 2 brings its own study screen and its own 2 minutes. Code words left over from Part 1 take up room the second screen needs. Start it from zero, as if Part 1 never happened.

tips.h: Trust the first match
tips.p: A set that matches your code at once is usually right. Doubt grows with staring, and the clock does not stop for it.

tips.h: Keep a rhythm of 10 seconds
tips.p: Twelve questions in 2 minutes is 10 seconds each. At the sixth question, Time Left should read about a minute. If it reads less, pick faster; a blank scores nothing, a guess may.

Reading all five options shape by shape before striking, when the first shape alone drops most of them.
Going back to a doubtful question and losing two or three fresh ones to the clock.

method.h: Find the anchor and the move
method.p: Read the direction to its end first. Every one has an anchor, a letter or a row, and a move: above, below, left, right or reverse order. Name both to yourself before your eyes drop to the table.

method.h: Fix the anchor on the table
method.p: Find the anchor letter and hold its row and column. If the direction names a row, count the Roman numerals downward, Row I first: Row I, Row II, Row III.

method.h: Make the move in your head
method.p: Above and below keep the column and move one row. Left and right keep the row. A reversed row reads right to left: its first letter becomes its last, and a middle letter stays put.

method.h: Check against the five options
method.p: The letter you reach must be one of the five options given with the question. If it is not, you have slipped a row or a column; read the direction once more and move again.

method.h: Click and keep your place
method.p: Click the letter and let your eye fall to the next direction, not back to the table. A question you were sure of is finished; look again only after the tenth.

tips.h: Read in the language you read faster
tips.p: Choose the line you read faster on the instruction screen and keep to it for all 10 questions. Switching between the Hindi and English lines mid-test costs seconds on every question.

tips.h: Treat 'directly' and 'only' as exact words
tips.p: Directly above means the same column, one row up, never diagonal. 'The only letter' promises a single answer; if two letters seem to fit, read the direction again and check your row and column.

tips.h: Number the rows before the first question
tips.p: On the instruction screen, give each row its Roman numeral, Row I first, and count the columns once. In the test a direction such as 'below C in Row II' then becomes a row number and a column number, and you stop counting under the clock.

tips.h: Split an 'if' direction into two halves
tips.p: Some directions carry a condition. Example: 'if D is right of C in Row IV, take the last letter; if not, the middle of Row III'. Settle the if first, with a plain yes or no. Only then read the half that applies.

tips.h: Keep to 30 seconds a question
tips.p: If a path is still lost after a second reading, click the likeliest letter and move on. Return at the end if the clock allows.

mistakes: Counting from the wrong end of a reversed row, so the answer lands one letter off.
Letting the eye slip a line and reading Row III when the direction says Row II.
Taking 'above' as the letter one row up and one column across, instead of the same column.
Reading the answer half of an 'if' direction before settling the if, and choosing the wrong half.
Letting one lost path take a full minute, so the last two questions get no click before the clock submits.
Practising only the Letter Table and meeting the Watch Table or the Number Table in the hall.

lines: Which number appears just opposite to the number between B3 and D2?
While moving from North to East by the shortest route, which number appears in between the two?
example.answer: The RDSO guideline's example gives 5 as the first answer and 2 as the second.

method.h: Read to the question mark
method.p: Read the whole direction before you touch the circle. Pick out the start, the way of travel, and what is asked at the end: between, opposite or the shortest route.

method.h: Place the start
method.p: Find the start on the circle: a letter with its number, such as B3, or a compass point, such as North. Hold that place with your eye; its own number is the answer only if the direction says so.

method.h: Travel one place at a time
method.p: Move round the circle place by place, noting the number at each place you pass. Right-handedly is clockwise, left-handedly anticlockwise. The place you start from is not your first step; the first step is the next place along.

method.h: Land on the right place
method.p: Between: take the place that lies between the two named places. Opposite: go four places on from there, either way round. Shortest route: count both ways round and take the shorter way. In every case the answer is the number in the square at the place where the direction lands.

method.h: Click and move on
method.p: Every question lists the same numbers as options, so a slip does not show there. Re-read the direction once, click, and drop to the next one. 20 questions in 10 minutes is 30 seconds each; no second visits until the end.

tips.h: Learn the compass before question one
tips.p: North sits at the top. Clockwise from there come North-East, East, South-East, South, South-West, West and North-West. Say them once on the instruction screen.

tips.h: Do not count the start as a step
tips.p: The place you start from is where you stand. Your first step is the next place along. Say the number at each place as you reach it, stop exactly where the direction says, and then read what the question asks there.

tips.h: Opposite is always four places on
tips.p: The circle has eight places, so the opposite place is four places away, whichever way you go. Count four once and stop; counting round both ways is how a place gets lost.

tips.h: Shortest route means the shorter arc
tips.p: Between North and East the shorter way round passes through one place, North-East, so the guideline's second example gives 2. When a direction says the shortest route, count both ways and take the fewer places.

tips.h: Answer with the number, not the letter
tips.p: B3 names the place lettered B whose square holds 3. The letters mark places; the numbers in the squares are the answers. A number can sit in more than one square, so read the square at the place you reached.

mistakes: Turning anticlockwise for 'right-handedly', or clockwise for 'left-handedly'.
Counting the start position as the first step.
Reading 'between' as 'next to'.
Answering with the letter at the stop, or the start's own number, instead of the number in the square you reached.
Going the long way round when the direction asks for the shortest route.
Leaving the last questions blank after a slow start.

lines: Which is the only number that appears directly above the number '1'?
example.answer: In the example of the RDSO guideline the answer is 2: the cell straight above the 1 holds a 2.

method.h: Hear the direction out
method.p: The grid can wait until the sentence is over. Note the number the direction names, and what it asks about it. That is a position such as directly above, a reversed row, or a path along cells.

method.h: Find the named number
method.p: Locate that number in the table. If it appears more than once, find every copy first and decide which one the direction means before you move.

method.h: Move with the rule
method.p: Above or below sends you up or down one column, never sideways. Left or right runs along one row. On a reversed row, read it backwards first, and only then make the move.

method.h: Read the cell, click the option
method.p: Read the number in the cell you reach, find it among the options and click it. Do not re-check unless time is left at the end.

tips.h: Read look-alike digits twice
tips.p: In a number table 1 and 7, 6 and 9, 3 and 8 sit close in shape. Read the digit in the cell you reach twice before you click.

tips.h: Reverse means mirror
tips.p: A reversed row is read from right to left. The two end cells swap, the next pair swaps, and so on in towards the middle. Picture the mirror; there is no time to rewrite the row.

tips.h: Turn the direction into a short code
tips.p: Before you look at the table, shrink the direction to a code: above 1, left of 7, row three reversed. Carry the code to the grid, not the sentence.

tips.h: Spend the 30 seconds on the cell, not the sentence
tips.p: 10 questions in 5 minutes is 30 seconds each. Read the direction once, well, and give the rest of the time to finding and checking the cell. A question that passes 30 seconds gets your likeliest number.

tips.h: Work the example on the instruction screen
tips.p: In the hall, read the example before you start. Find its answer in the table yourself, so that question 1 is not your first look at the grid.

mistakes: Sliding along the row for above or below, when the answer sits in the column.
Taking the first copy of a repeated number without checking the other copies.
Reading a reversed row from its old left end and landing on the mirror cell.
Reading one long direction three times and spending the whole 30 seconds on it.
Letting the eye slip one cell sideways and clicking the neighbour's number.
Leaving a question blank because the direction looked odd; a marked guess costs nothing.

intro: The Brick Test is kind 3a of the Depth Perception Test, Test 3 of the RRB ALP CBAT. In the hall it gives 50 questions in 5 minutes: ten piles of bricks, five lettered bricks in each. Every brick in a pile has the same size and shape. Your job is to count how many bricks touch each lettered brick, including the ones the drawing hides. introHi: ईंट परीक्षण (3a) RRB ALP CBAT के तीसरे टेस्ट, गहराई बोध परीक्षण, का एक प्रकार है। परीक्षा हॉल में 5 मिनट में 50 सवाल आते हैं: एक ही आकार की ईंटों का ढेर दिखता है, कुछ ईंटों पर A से E तक अक्षर लिखे हैं, और हर अक्षर वाली ईंट को छूती ईंटें गिननी हैं, छिपी ईंटें भी। यह टेस्ट देखता है कि आप सपाट चित्र से ढेर की गहराई, यानी पीछे और नीचे की ईंटें, कितनी सही समझते हैं।

how.p: The test opens with its rules in Hindi and English and an example pile with its five answers. On the portal this screen allows 5 minutes; Skip Instruction starts the test sooner.

A pile is drawn on the left. On the right are questions 1 to 5, one for each letter A to E, with a row of numbers. If the row runs past the screen's edge, the scrollbar brings the rest into view, as in the hall.

how.h: Click the count, then Save & Next
how.p: For each letter, click the number that matches your count. Save & Next opens the next pile; the numbering continues 6 to 10, and so on up to 50.

lines: In the pile shown in the RDSO guideline, brick A touches two other bricks, D and E.
Bricks B, C, D and E touch 3, 3, 4 and 4 bricks.
example.answer: So the answers are A 2, B 3, C 3, D 4, E 4.

method.h: Read the pile before the letters
method.p: Spend the first two or three seconds on the whole pile. See how many layers it has, which bricks lie along and which across, and where one brick rests on two below. The letters make sense only once the structure is clear.

method.h: Go around the lettered brick in six directions
method.p: Above, below, left, right, front, back: the same order every time. On each side count every brick in contact, not just one. A brick lying across others may rest on two or three below, and all of them touch it.

method.h: Add the bricks you cannot see
method.p: A brick cannot float. If a brick sits above the bottom layer and nothing shows beneath it, a hidden brick holds it up, and it counts.

method.h: Count once, click, move on
method.p: Say the number, click it, go to the next letter. Recount only when a contact you already found for another letter is missing from this count. Five letters share one pile, so your picture of it carries over from A to E.

tips.h: Touch means a face or an edge
tips.p: A brick that shares a face with the lettered brick, or lies along one of its edges, counts as touching. One that meets it only at a corner point does not.

tips.h: Use the answers you already have
tips.p: Touching works both ways. If A touches D and E, then A is already one of D's bricks and one of E's. Note which lettered bricks touch each other before you count, and carry those contacts across the five answers.

tips.h: Keep to 30 seconds a pile
tips.p: Fifty questions in 5 minutes is 6 seconds a question, or 30 seconds a pile. If a pile passes 30 seconds, mark your working answers and move.

tips.h: One direction at a time
tips.p: Finish each of the six directions before you start the next. A brick lying across the top may also meet the front or back edge. Count it in the first direction where you meet it, then skip it. No brick is counted twice.

tips.h: Sit it with a mouse and a scrollbar
tips.p: In the hall you answer at a desktop with a mouse. The rows of numbers may run past the right edge, and you reach them with the scrollbar. Practise on a laptop or desktop so the scroll and click become habit.

mistakes: Counting only the bricks you can see and forgetting the hidden one holding a brick up.
Counting the same brick twice because it touches on a face and also along an edge.
Counting a brick that meets the lettered brick only at a corner point.
Clicking B's count in C's row, so two answers go wrong from one slip.
Recounting a pile three times for one doubtful letter and leaving the last piles blank.

Open the review. For each wrong letter, find the direction you missed: above, below, left, right, front or back. Use that order on every pile from now on.
Hidden bricks only. In the review, mark every brick held up by something you cannot see. Sit a second paper and count the hidden supports first.
Pace. Sit a paper at 30 seconds a pile and reach the tenth pile with time on the clock. Accuracy may dip today; reaching question 50 is the goal.
Mutual touching. Before counting, list the pairs of lettered bricks that touch each other, then check that each pair shows in both answers. One paper, then review.
Two papers on a laptop or desktop, using the scrollbar. Compare the two T-Scores and review every wrong count, not only the ones you guessed.
Sit the free Full Mock on a laptop. Test 3 comes third, so you meet it with some tiredness, as in the hall. Check the T-Score of Test 3 against the target of 60.

faq.q: How many questions are in the RRB ALP Brick Test and how much time do I get?
faq.a: 50 questions in 5 minutes: ten piles, five lettered bricks in each. That is 6 seconds a question, or 30 seconds a pile, on one clock for the whole test.

faq.q: ALP brick test kaise hota hai: what is asked in the Brick Test?
faq.a: A pile of same-size bricks is drawn; five carry the letters A to E. For each lettered brick you count how many bricks touch it, hidden ones included, and click that number beside the letter.

faq.q: Do hidden bricks count in the Brick Test?
faq.a: Yes. If a brick in an upper layer has nothing visible under it, a hidden brick holds it up, and that brick counts. Count a hidden brick only when the drawing shows it must be there.

faq.q: Does a brick that touches only at a corner count in the Brick Test?
faq.a: No. Contact means a shared face or a shared edge. Bricks that meet at a single corner point are not touching. A brick that touches on two sides is still counted once.

faq.q: Is the Brick Test still asked if the last exam gave the Hidden Cube Test?
faq.a: Yes. Test 3 opens as either kind, and the choice is not announced. In the last exam (CEN 01/2024) the hall gave the Hidden Cube Test, as the institute's records show. The Brick Test remains the other kind, and the faster one: 5 minutes against 10.

introHi: RRB ALP CBAT के तीसरे टेस्ट, गहराई बोध परीक्षण, में परीक्षा हॉल दो में से एक प्रकार देता है; छिपे घन परीक्षण (3b) उनमें से एक है। इसमें 10 मिनट में 50 सवाल होते हैं और हर सवाल में गुटकों का एक ढेर दिखता है। गिनना उन गुटकों को है जिनकी कोई सतह, कोई किनारा या कोई कोना नहीं दिखता, यानी जो चित्र में हैं तो ज़रूर, पर नज़र नहीं आते।

lines: In Practice Problem I of the RDSO guideline, two blocks are completely hidden: no side or corner of either shows.
Practice Problems II and III follow on the same instruction screen.
example.answer: The RDSO guideline's answers are 2, 4 and 3.

method.h: Set the back row first
method.p: The RDSO guideline's rule: the base of the farthest row always has three blocks. Place that row in your mind before anything else. It fixes how deep the pile goes and how much can stand behind what you see.

method.h: Build the pile layer by layer
method.p: Start at the bottom layer and work up. Every block above the base needs a block beneath it, so the drawing proves blocks it does not show. Fix each layer in your mind, hidden blocks included; you test them in the next two steps.

method.h: Shortlist the inside
method.p: A block is hidden only when covered on three sides: on top, in front and on the side you look at. So the front row, the highest layer and the end of every row on the side you see are out. Only the inside blocks remain.

method.h: Test the shortlist
method.p: Ask of each block: does any part of it reach your eye? A sliver of an edge or the tip of a corner puts it out. Count the blocks where the answer is no, click that number, move on.

tips.h: Do not total the pile
tips.p: The answer is the hidden count alone. Counting every block and then subtracting the visible ones doubles the work and the slips. Go straight to the blocks the pile encloses and test only those.

tips.h: Count the back row before the front
tips.p: The farthest row has three blocks at its base, even when the blocks in front hide them all. Any of those three with a block in front, above and on its open side is hidden. Forget the row and you miss them.

tips.h: Twelve seconds, then the next pile
tips.p: Twelve seconds is one pile. A pile that passes it gets your closest count and a move on; the clock does not wait for a recount. An answer always beats a blank.

tips.h: Keep this test apart from the Brick Test
tips.p: You prepare both kinds of Test 3. The Brick Test asks how many bricks touch a lettered brick; this one asks how many blocks are completely covered. Fix the rule on the instruction screen and keep to it for all 50 piles.

tips.h: Land every click on its own line
tips.p: Several piles share one screen, so pile 7's count can land on pile 8's line. Put the pointer on the line, glance at its pile once more, then click. This is mouse work; sit the papers on a laptop or desktop, not a phone.

mistakes: Counting a block as hidden when its top edge or one corner still shows.
Leaving out the three base blocks of the farthest row because the rows in front hide them.
Using the Brick Test's touching rule here and counting neighbours instead of covered blocks.
Clicking the number on another pile's line, since several piles share a screen.
Chasing one doubtful block through three rebuilds of the pile while the final part of the paper goes unanswered.

faq.q: How long is the Hidden Cube Test, and how many piles come in it?
faq.a: 50 questions in 10 minutes, one pile a question, on one Time Left clock. That is 12 seconds a pile, or 5 piles a minute.

faq.q: Hidden cube test kaise hota hai? What does one question look like on screen?
faq.a: Each question shows a pile of blocks of one size and shape. You count the blocks the others hide on every side, no face, edge or corner showing, and click that number.

faq.q: Which blocks count as hidden in the Hidden Cube Test?
faq.a: Hidden means nothing of the block can be seen. A block on top, a block in front and a block on its open side cover it fully. The RDSO guideline's first practice pile has two such blocks.

faq.q: Can a block in the bottom layer be hidden?
faq.a: Yes. A base block is hidden when a block sits on it, one stands in front and one closes its open side. The farthest row's three base blocks are often hidden this way.

faq.q: Will the hall give the Hidden Cube Test or the Brick Test for Test 3?
faq.a: One of the two; you do not know in advance. In the last exam (CEN 01/2024) the hall gave the Hidden Cube Test, as the institute's records show. Prepare both.

intro: The Yes or No Test is kind 4a of the Power of Observation Test, Test 4 of the RRB ALP CBAT. The hall gives 96 questions in 4 minutes on one Time Left clock. Each question is a pair of numbers side by side. You mark Y if the two numbers are the same and N if they differ. Nothing is worked out; the digits are only read and matched. The test measures how fast and how surely your eyes catch a changed or swapped digit.

On screen the pairs sit in rows, one to a row, with a Y and an N beside each. You read the left number, read the right number, click Y or N and move to the next row. Save & Next carries you to the next part of the list. This page gives the screen flow, the RDSO guideline's example, a reading method, the costly mistakes and a 7-day plan. This portal has practice papers for it and one free Full Mock after login.
introHi: हाँ या नहीं परीक्षण RRB ALP CBAT के चौथे टेस्ट, अवलोकन शक्ति परीक्षण का 4a प्रकार है। परीक्षा हॉल में 96 सवाल 4 मिनट में एक ही Time Left घड़ी पर आते हैं; हर सवाल में दो संख्याएँ आमने-सामने होती हैं और बताना होता है कि दोनों एक जैसी हैं (Y) या अलग (N)। कुछ जोड़ना-घटाना नहीं है; यह टेस्ट मापता है कि आपकी आँखें बदले हुए या आपस में उलटे अंक को कितनी तेज़ी और सटीकता से पकड़ती हैं।
answerStyle: Y and N beside each pair; click Y if the two numbers are the same, N if they differ.

how.p: The test opens with instructions in Hindi and English and five example pairs, answered Y, N, N, Y and N. The portal's screen allows 5 minutes; press Skip Instruction when ready.
The pairs come in rows, 24 to a part, each row with its own Y and N. One Time Left clock of 4 minutes runs over all 96 questions.
Read the left number, then the right one. Click Y if they are the same, N if they differ. Each click is kept the moment you make it.
Save & Next brings the next part of 24; four parts make the 96 questions. The clock keeps running while the screen changes.
Press Submit after the last part, or the clock submits at zero. On the portal the T-Score appears at once, with a review of every pair and its correct letter.

example.answer: The answers are Y, N, N, Y and N.

method.h: Read the left number in chunks of three
method.p: Take the left number in groups of three digits and see each group as one block: 487 562. A chunk of three is one picture for the eye, easier to hold than six loose digits. A four-digit number splits into two chunks of two, a five-digit one into two and three.

method.h: Read the right number in the same chunks
method.p: Read the right number the same way: 487 652. Match chunk against chunk, in order. The moment one differs, stop reading; the answer is already N.

method.h: Click the letter and leave the row
method.p: Every chunk the same is Y; any chunk different is N. Click the letter on that row and move to the next pair without a second look.

method.h: Hold one rhythm
method.p: Read, read, click, next. The rhythm matters more than any single pair. A steady rhythm reaches the last part; a stop-start one leaves it blank.

tips.h: Short pairs are not a rest
tips.p: 589 against 589 takes one chunk, but the next row may hold six digits. Do not let a run of short pairs set a glance pace that you carry into the long ones.

tips.h: Expect two neighbours swapped
tips.p: Two of the three N pairs in the example swap two neighbouring digits, like 2768 against 2786. Same digits, same length, same look at a glance. Only a chunk read shows the changed order.

tips.h: The last digit is the easiest to miss
tips.p: 36463 against 36462 differs only at the end, where the eye is already leaving for the next row. Read the final chunk in full. The first digit deserves the same care.

tips.h: Hold 24 a minute, never re-check
tips.p: 96 questions in 4 minutes is 24 a minute, two and a half seconds a pair. Trust the first careful read. A hurried second read adds doubt and eats the next pair's time.

tips.h: Keep the pointer on your row
tips.p: With 24 rows to a part, eyes slip a line and the click lands on the wrong row. Keep the pointer on the row you are reading; the letter then goes where the eye is.

mistakes: Judging a pair by its length alone, when every pair in the example has the same length on both sides.
Missing two swapped neighbours in the middle of a six-digit number.
Clicking the Y or N of the row above after the eyes jump a line.
Reading the numbers as amounts, in thousands and lakhs, instead of as strings of digits.
Slowing to a crawl after one doubtful pair and losing three or four pairs to the clock.
Leaving the last part untouched when Time Left runs down, instead of clicking a letter on every row.

plan.task: Work the five example pairs by hand, saying each chunk aloud. Sit one practice paper on a laptop to meet the rows, the Y and N and the 4-minute clock.
Open the review of Day 1. Sort every wrong pair: a swap missed, an end digit missed or a click on the wrong row.
Sit a fresh paper reading in chunks of three only. Accept a slower pace today; accuracy first, speed after.

method.p: A count of one means you missed a place; a count above four means you counted a place twice. Re-walk once. Otherwise click the radio and move to the next picture without a second look.

tips.h: Count places, not figures
tips.p: Do not ask which figure moved. Ask, at each place, whether set B holds the same figure as set A. The number of mismatched places is the answer.

tips.h: The count is never one
tips.p: The RDSO guideline gives the choices as no difference, or two, three or four figures moved. There is no option for one. If your count is one, a second mismatch is waiting; look again.

tips.h: Stop at four
tips.p: Four mismatches is D, and the count cannot go higher. The moment you reach four, click D and move on; the rest of the places do not matter.

tips.h: Click A only after a full pass
tips.p: A question that looks the same at a glance still needs the full walk. Click A only when a full pass finds zero mismatches. That pass costs a few seconds and saves the mark.

tips.h: Keep to 7 seconds a question
tips.p: 60 questions in 7 minutes is 7 seconds each. One walk, one click, Save & Next. If a question fights you, click your count and move on.

mistakes: Hunting for the figure that moved instead of walking the places in order, which wastes seconds and loses the count.
Stopping at one mismatch and clicking B without finding the second.
Clicking A after a glance, when the mismatch sits at the far end of the set.

method.h: Name one feature of the figure
method.p: Look at figure a for a moment and name the one thing that sets it apart. It may be the slant of a line, a notch, a dot or a cut corner. Do not study the whole figure.

method.h: Sweep the five for that feature only
method.p: Run your eye along A to E and ask one question of each: does it have the feature? Options without the feature drop out. If one option is left, click it; if more than one is left, go to the next step.

method.h: Settle a tie with a second feature

method.h: Click, then drop one row

tips.h: Let the five options tell you the feature

tips.h: Keep the row
tips.p: Figure c always goes with the third question of the sheet, whatever its number, 3, 7 or 71. One slipped row spoils every answer after it on that sheet. Say the row's letter to yourself before each click.

tips.h: No second look at a finished sheet

faq.a: Stop comparing whole figures. Fix one anchor feature, sweep A to E on that alone, and click. Sit practice papers with the 8-minute clock until the sweep fits inside 7 seconds.

summaryHi: समान आकृति परीक्षण में एक आकृति दी होती है और उसके नीचे या बगल में A से E तक पाँच आकृतियाँ; उनमें से बिल्कुल समान एक चुननी है। परीक्षा हॉल में 72 सवाल 8 मिनट में आते हैं, यानी हर मिनट 9 सवाल। तरीका यह है: दी गई आकृति को एक बार देखें, उसकी एक पहचान तय करें, और सिर्फ़ उसी पहचान पर पाँचों विकल्प देखें। आईने जैसी उलटी आकृति या बिंदु हटी हुई आकृति गलत विकल्प है, और हर क्लिक से पहले सवाल का नंबर देख लें। पिछली परीक्षा (CEN 01/2024) में हॉल ने टेस्ट 5 के लिए यही प्रकार दिया था, जैसा संस्थान के रिकॉर्ड बताते हैं। इस पोर्टल पर हॉल की गिनती और घड़ी वाले प्रैक्टिस पेपर हैं, लॉगिन के बाद एक मुफ़्त फुल मॉक है और सबमिट करते ही T-Score दिखता है; लक्ष्य हर टेस्ट में T-Score 60 रखें, पास के लिए 42 चाहिए।
